                                        PROJECT NO. 58482

 LARGE LOAD DEMAND                                §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 MANAGEMENT SERVICE                               §               OF TEXAS

               TEXAS INDUSTRIAL ENERGY CONSUMERS' COMMENTS

                                       I.      INTRODUCTION

       Texas Industrial Energy Consumers (TIEC) appreciates the opportunity to provide

comments on the Proposal for Publication (PFP) of new §25.521 relating to the Large Load

Demand Management Service (LLDMS) in Project No. 58482. TIEC' s members are among the

large electricity users who proposed this service previously at the Commission and ultimately as

part of Senate Bill 6 (SB 6). Many industrial sites are not flexible and do not typically participate

in the wholesale market but are able to reduce their usage in advance of an emergency event with

sufficient notice. This notice allows users to pre-position site personnel and adjust site operations

to achieve an orderly ramp down over a longer period, which is not currently facilitated by existing

services with deployment times at thirty minutes or less.       During extreme weather events-

including Winter Storm Elliott (December 2022), Winter Storm Heather (January 2024), and

Winter Storm Fern (January 2026)-large industrial loads voluntarily curtailed at the request of

the Commission and ERCOT, and this demand response was acknowledged as helping maintain

reliability. TIEC envisions LLDMS as formalizing these types of voluntary communications and

activities into a structured market service.

       TIEC appreciates that the proposed rule adopts an "as-needed" procurement model

consistent with TIEC' s prior recommendation, under which ERCOT would generally procure

participation ahead of an identified extreme weather event only if needed.         TIEC offers the

following comments on Staff' s specific questions and the proposed rule text.




                                                  1
                         II.   RESPONSES TO STAFF'S QUESTIONS

1.     Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling entity
       representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to deploy but is
       subject to availability verification during the Large Load Demand Management
       Service (LLDMS) obligation period. Should a large load customer that is available
       but not ultimately instructed to deploy during the LLDMS obligation period be
       compensated some percentage of the market clearing price for the large load
       customer's availability to reduce demand during the LLDMS obligation period? If
       so, what is an appropriate payment to the large load customer for their availability
       during the LLDMS obligation period?

       Generally, TIEC envisioned that this service would pay for actual deployments, not

"availability" to deploy. This approach would produce the lowest cost for consumers paying for

the service and avoid payments in seasons or years when the service is not needed. Paying loads

for being available would introduce a standing cost that is somewhat at odds with the fundamental

cost advantages of an event-driven design. It could also create adverse incentives by allowing

loads to pre-qualify and collect availability payments without genuine operational readiness, which

is something that has been previously encountered in the Emergency Response Service (ER S)

context.   Tying compensation to actual curtailment aligns payment with performance and the

service's intended incremental reliability value. Verifying true availability is also more difficult

than verifying actual curtailment.

       That being said, TIEC recognizes that if the service is deployed very infrequently, and there

is no compensation outside of deployment periods, customers may not invest in resources to

participate. For this reason, TIEC is not requesting but is not opposed to a modest availability

payment to incentivize pre-qualification and participation. If an availability payment is adopted,

availability verification must be rigorous and enforceable, and the Commission should retain

flexibility to revisit the percentage after gaining operational experience to determine whether it

appropriately incentivizes participation without imposing unnecessary costs on the market. For



                                                 2
 this reason, it might be efficient to not specify the percentage in the rule but allow ERCOT to

change the percentage (or eliminate it) based on experience with the service. TIEC also notes that

the costs associated with this percentage will depend on the offer cap that is ultimately adopted

and as discussed below, TIEC does not believe that a $5,000/MWh offer cap will elicit meaningful

participation. TIEC would prefer a very low percentage (or zero) availability payment if necessary

to support a higher deployment payment.

2.     Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a calendar
       year. What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

       In prior comments, TIEC suggested an annual budget of approximately $50 million based

on the assumption that the service would be used at most once per year, with a potential increase

to $60-75 million to provide headroom for multiple deployments in a single year. So, the proposed

$54 million annual cap falls within this range and is reasonable as an initial budget.

       However, TIEC reiterates that the budget should be understood as a ceiling, not an

expected annual expenditure .      Given the service ' s infrequent , event - driven nature , actual

spending in most years should be well below the cap. The $54 million figure provides sufficient

headroom for effective deployment during extreme weather events while limiting exposure for

consumers and retail entities.

       Additionally, the Commission should build in a mechanism for periodic review of the

budget cap to ensure it remains appropriately calibrated. If operational experience demonstrates

that the budget is either insufficient to procure adequate resources during extreme events or

unnecessarily high relative to actual deployment costs, the Commission should adjust accordingly.




                                                 3
 3.     What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and how
       far in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?

       ERCOT should use a tiered approach to assessment and procurement that begins

engagement early, as an extreme weather event becomes increasingly likely. Extreme winter

storms are particularly well-suited to this procurement model because they are typically discrete,

identifiable, and forecastable well in advance, providing the lead time large industrial facilities

need to make informed participation decisions.

       The procurement triggers in proposed subsection (d)(1)(A)-(D) provide an appropriate

framework for this tiered approach. Early engagement is critical for the large industrial loads this

service is designed to attract. These are complex facilities where curtailment involves significant

operational, safety, and business considerations. Advance notice is necessary to deploy additional

personnel, initiate orderly ramp-down processes, and adjust operations without compromising

safety, product quality, or equipment integrity. ERCOT should ideally begin issuing requests for

proposals as early as practicable once probabilistic modeling or weather forecasting identifies an

elevated risk-ideally no less than 48 to 72 hours before an anticipated EEA event when forecast

confidence supports such lead time. Combined with at least 24-hour advance notice to the QSE

required before deployment under subsection (e)(1), this timing would give loads sufficient time

to evaluate their operational circumstances, submit offers, and prepare for curtailment.

       TIEC further recommends that ERCOT develop clear, transparent criteria for when each

procurement trigger is activated, so that potential participants can anticipate when the auction

process may begin and plan accordingly.

       Although the weekly trigger in subsection (d)(1)(B) appropriately limits procurement to

the forecasted week based on weekly weather forecasting, the monthly trigger in subsection



                                                 4
 (d)(1)(A) contains no comparable lead-time constraint.         TIEC recommends that subsection

(d)(1)(A) be revised to clarify that procurement under the monthly probabilistic modeling trigger

is permitted only on a month-ahead basis, meaning no earlier than one month prior to the modeled

month, and based on monthly forecasts. This revision would make subsection (d)(1)(A) consistent

with subsection (d)(1)(B), which expressly links the weekly trigger to weekly forecasts. Without

this limitation, ERCOT could use monthly modeling to justify procuring LLDMS well in advance,

potentially on a seasonal or annual basis, which would be inconsistent with the service's as-needed

procurement model.

4.     Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If so,
       what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

       Deploying LLDMS for transmission emergencies does not appear appropriate unless the

transmission emergency is tied to an extreme weather event. In TIEC's prior comments, TIEC

emphasized that PURA § 39.170(b)(1) limits the deployment ofthe large load management service

to "extreme weather events," and that the Legislature' s prescriptive language indicates the service

is not meant to be a standing tool available for all categories of grid stress. Extending the service

to transmission emergencies that are unrelated to weather events would effectively repurpose it for

conditions that existing market tools are better suited to address.

        The proposed rule already defines "extreme weather condition" as a weather condition that

creates a significant risk for an EEA event. A transmission emergency-defined in subsection

(b)(4) as a condition in which a transmission element is operating above its emergency rating

creating a significant risk of firm load shed-may or may not be weather-related.           Allowing

deployment for transmission emergencies that are not caused by extreme weather conditions would

exceed the statutory authority granted under PURA § 39.170(b) and would blur the clear boundary

the Legislature established for this service.

                                                  5
         PURA § 39.170(b)(1) limits the deployment of the large load management service to

" extreme weather events ." Specifically , PURA states , " the rules governing this service nlust

specify the periods when the service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during

extreme weather events." 1 The directive to "specify the periods when the service may be used"

requires ERCOT to define the particular types of extreme weather events where it may deploy the

service. It is not meant to be a standing tool available at all times or for all categories of grid stress

like other ancillary services, but it must be tied to identifiable weather events. Had the Legislature

intended ERCOT to deploy the service in anticipation oftransmission emergencies that may result

in entering into an energy emergency alert, it would not have used such prescriptive language.

        Moreover, from a practical standpoint, transmission emergencies often arise and resolve

more quickly than the 24-hour notice period contemplated by the service's design. The large

industrial loads targeted by this service are not well-positioned to respond to localized transmission

constraints that may arise and dissipate within hours. These loads require significant lead time to

curtail safely; and deploying them for transient transmission issues could impose unnecessary costs

and operational disruption without commensurate reliability benefits.

        If the Commission nevertheless determines that some form of transmission emergency

deployment is appropriate, TIEC recommends at minimum the following limitations: (1)

deployment should be limited to transmission emergencies that are caused by or coincide with an

extreme weather condition; (2) the 24-hour advance notice requirement must still apply; and (3)

the budget for transmission emergency deployments should be separate from and additional to the

budget for weather-related deployments, so that the primary purpose of the service is not diluted.




        1 PURA § 39.170(b) (emphasis added).

                                                    6
                                 III.    GENERAL COMMENTS

A.     The proposed offer cap should be significantly increased to reflect that this is an as-
       needed service where compensation is primarily deployment-driven, unlike other
       reliability or ancillary services.

       The proposed rule establishes an offer cap of $5,000/MWh in subsection (d)(3)(B)(v). That

cap is too low to attract meaningful participation from eligible large industrial loads and could

undermine LLDMS. It equals the ERCOT system-wide energy-market offer cap, which fails to

account for the economics of participation by the loads this service is intended to attract.

       Large, inflexible loads are unlikely to bid into a service capped at $5,000/MWh because

they could obtain the same net avoided costs by curtailing when wholesale prices are high.

LLDMS is intended to attract loads that do not otherwise participate in the wholesale market-

loads that are neither price-responsive nor participants in other reliability or ancillary services. If

LLDMS compensation does not exceed the value available from curtailing during high-price

intervals, there is little incentive to undertake its commitments, including pre-qualification,

availability verification, and deployment on ERCOT' s instruction. A $5,000/MWh cap would

therefore make LLDMS compensation indistinguishable from the energy-market price signal and

defeat the purpose of a separate service.

       The Commission should consider significantly increasing the offer cap to -$20,000/MWh.

This offer cap is grounded in the system-wide Value of Lost Load (VOLL), which represents the

cost to consumers of involuntary load shedding and provides an appropriate analytical foundation

for determining the value of voluntary demand reductions that help prevent such outcomes. TIEC

recognizes that many large customers participate in other ancillary services and reliability services

that are capped at $5,000/MWh, but those services make availability payments.             As a result,

customers generally forecast the anticipated availability payments over time against their cost if


                                                  7
 they were deployed to decide whether it is economic to participate. For an "as needed" service

where the payments are primarily or exclusively deployment-based, this $5,000/MWh cap will not

cover the value of curtailing for the types of loads this service was intended to attract.

        The offer cap should fall somewhere between the system-wide energy market offer cap of

$5,000/MWh and the system-wide VOLL of $35,000/MWh. A cap at or below $5,000/MWh

provides no incremental incentive beyond what the energy market already offers.                            The

Commission's VOLL study found that medium and large commercial and industrial customers

had a VOLL of approximately $22,721/MWh for one hour of unserved energy. 2 This empirical

data point confirms that a cap in the $20,000 to $25,000/MWh range would reflect the significant

economic loss for large industrial loads during curtailment-including lost production, restart

costs, potential equipment damage, and contractual disruption-while remaining within

reasonable bounds for consumer cost impacts.

        An appropriately calibrated offer cap is essential to the success ofthis program. If the cap

is set too low, participation will be minimal, and the service will fail to achieve its statutory purpose

of maintaining reliability during extreme weather events.               This concern is not speculative.

ERCOT' s Summer 2024 Contracts for Capacity RFP-which similarly sought demand response

from non-price-responsive loads-was ultimately unsuccessful, receiving offers from only two

QSEs totaling 21.5 MW of capacity with only 6.5 MW that could potentially qualify.3 While that

RFP did not include a 24-hour notice requirement or an extreme weather event limitation, it is




        2 Review of Value of Lost Load in the ERCOT Market , Project No . 55837 , Staff' s Final Recommendation
on         VOLL           at         3         (August        22,          2024)             (available      at:
https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/Documents/55837_13_1422000.PDF).
         3 Energy Choice Matters , ERCOT Cancels Summer Capacity RFP ( June 21 , 2024 ) ( available at :
https://www.energychoicematters.com/stories/20240621c.html).

                                                       8
 illustrative of the limited participation that results when compensation does not adequately reflect

the costs and risks of curtailment for large industrial facilities.

        TIEC recognizes that a higher offer cap raises questions about cost containment. However,

the annual budget cap in subsection (f)(4) already provides an overall ceiling on program

expenditures. The offer cap and the budget cap serve complementary but distinct functions: the

budget cap limits total spending, while the offer cap determines whether the service can attract

sufficient participation to fulfill its reliability purpose. A higher offer cap does not necessarily

mean higher total costs-it means that participants can submit offers reflecting their true cost of

curtailment, which in turn enables a competitive procurement process that should yield efficient

market-clearing prices below the cap. Conversely, an artificially low offer cap will suppress

participation, undermining the obj ectives of the service.

B.      The Commission should avoid over-exclusion that would deter participation and
        undermine the program's effectiveness.

        Subsection (c)(2) enumerates several categories of ineligibility beyond those specified in

PURA § 39.170(b)(3). The purpose of these statutory exclusions is to ensure that LLDMS only

compensates loads for incremental, verifiable load reductions directly resulting from the service's

deployment, and not for reductions that would have occurred anyway due to price response or

participation in other services. The Commission should tailor any exclusions to capture loads that

are already likely to curtail before or during an extreme weather event, while avoiding over-

exclusion that would deter participation and undermine the program's effectiveness. Critically,

the Commission should also ensure that ineligibility is applied at the appropriate level of

granularity-at the MW level rather than the site level-so that non-participating capacity at a site

is not unnecessarily swept into an exclusion.



                                                    9
        Regarding the definition of "curtails in response to the wholesale price of electricity" under

PURA § 39.170(b)(3) and the proposed rule's price responsive test in subsection (c)(1)(B),

ERCOT should look for a pattern of significant price-responsive curtailment and not isolated

instances. In its Summer 2024 Contractsfor Capacio' Governing Document, ERCOT determined

that a site was price-responsive if it reduced its load by greater than 5% on average during 25% of

high price days (i.e., days when prices were more than $500 for four or more consecutive

intervals). 4 A similar, data-driven structure could be adopted here to ensure that customers with a

statistically significant relationship between elevated prices and lower load are identified as price-

responsive and excluded, while customers without that persistent pattern remain eligible. This

approach avoids disqualifying large industrial loads based on coincidental or de minimis

reductions that do not reflect systematic price response.

       TIEC does not believe it is necessary for a load to demonstrate that it requires a full 24

hours to ramp down safely in order to participate. PURA §39.170(b)(2) requires ERCOT to

provide at least 24 hours' advance notice before deployment, but the statute does not require a 24-

hour ramp-down period. In many instances, the actual curtailment will not take 24 hours, but

preparatory site activities need to be initiated up to 24 hours in advance. Qualification should

focus on whether the load can reduce consumption with advance notice to reach the committed

curtailment level safely.     This could be accomplished through limited testing, narrative

explanations of site curtailment procedures, or enrollment with a QSE and a straightforward

attestation that the site has a protocol in place to meet the program' s deployment parameters.

Because the service primarily compensates based on actual curtailment performance and on an as-




       4 ERCOT, Summer 2024 Contracts for Capacity Governing Document (May 29,2024) at 9.

                                                  10
 needed basis, there is no need for the rigorous eligibility requirements used for other ancillary or

reliability services that receive advance capacity payments.

       The Commission and ERCOT should ensure that any price-responsiveness test does not

inadvertently exclude loads that curtailed in response to a request from the Commission or ERCOT

for voluntary conservation during previous extreme weather events. The LLDMS is designed to

formalize the types of communications and activities that have historically been done on an ad

hoc, voluntary basis with industrial sites ahead of emergency conditions. If loads that responded

to those voluntary requests are deemed "price-responsive" and excluded, the program would

perversely disqualify the very participants whose past behavior demonstrates both willingness and

capability to provide the service.

       Response to transmission scarcity signals such as four coincident peak (4CP) or a successor

methodology should also not preclude participation in LLDMS. The goal of the service is to

procure curtailments that the market would not otherwise elicit due to price response or

participation in other services. Today, 4CP does not reliably align with net peak load or emergency

conditions. The absolute highest demand on the system (i.e., a 4CP interval) often occurs without

high wholesale market prices or diminished reserves. As a result, a customer who responds to 4CP

may not necessarily curtail during an emergency, so there is less likely to be any "double-dipping"

as there may be with customers that are price-responsive or participate in other ancillary services.

       Further, many large industrial loads may exhibit some limited response to a signal like 4CP

but could provide additional, distinct curtailment through LLDMS. Because 4CP management

and LLDMS deployment respond to fundamentally different conditions-peak-demand intervals

versus extreme-weather emergencies-4CP participation does not implicate the statutory concern

about compensating loads for reductions that would have occurred anyway. Excluding these loads

                                                 11
 would shrink the participant pool without reducing the risk of paying for non-incremental

reductions. 4CP participation should not, standing alone, render a customer ineligible.


       TIEC recommends no additional exclusions beyond those in PURA § 39.170(b)(3) for

price-responsive loads and loads that participate in other reliability or ancillary services. The

proposed rule's ineligibility list in subsection (c)(2) is already extensive.       Each additional

exclusion narrows the participant pool and increases the risk that ERCOT cannot procure sufficient

megawatts when LLDMS is most needed.


       Notably, subsection (c)(2) currently disqualifies a large load customer at the site level if it

participates in any of the enumerated services or programs. TIEC recommends refining these

provisions so that ineligibility applies only to the MWs at a site that participate in the relevant

excluded service, rather than rendering the entire site ineligible. A large industrial site may have

some MWs enrolled in an ancillary service or other excluded program while other MWs at the

same site are not participating in any excluded service and could provide incremental, verifiable

demand reductions through LLDMS. This MW-level approach would maximize the participant

pool and available megawatts without undermining the statutory goal of preventing double-

compensation because only the non-participating MWs would be eligible for LLDMS.


C.     The draft rule's definition of"extreme weather condition" is overly broad.

       The proposed rule defines "extreme weather condition" as "[al weather condition that

creates a significant risk for an energy emergency alert (EEA) event." The definition should be

narrowed to a "discrete weather event," which should primarily be extreme winter storms.

       Winter events pose the greatest reliability risk to the ERCOT system today and are typically

discrete, identifiable, and forecastable well in advance. A major winter storm can be forecast days

ahead, facilitating the 24-hour notice contemplated by subsection (e)(1). Large load customers

                                                 12
 can plan and execute an orderly curtailment as a named or forecasted winter storm approaches,

unlike during less predictable conditions. Summer heat, by contrast, is predictable, persistent, and

better suited to existing ancillary services and reliability mechanisms.

       A limited, bright-line standard requiring a discrete weather event would reserve LLDMS

for genuinely extreme conditions rather than routine deployment. This should be a resiliency

service, not a tool for managing predictable weather patterns. The ERCOT market already has

ancillary services and reliability mechanisms for non-weather contingencies and routine seasonal

conditions.   Extending LLDMS to any weather condition that elevates EEA risk-including

ordinary summer heat coinciding with high demand-would repurpose the service for conditions

those tools address better. It would also deter large industrial facilities with long curtailment lead

times and complex restart procedures from participating in a service covering such a broad range

of conditions.

       A narrower definition would also support the as-needed model' s cost-containment

objectives. As proposed, ERCOT could initiate procurement under subsection (d)(1) for any

weather condition creating "a significant risk" of an EEA event, potentially triggering procurement

frequently during summer. More frequent procurement would increase costs and erode the as-

needed model' s advantage over a seasonal service. If unchanged, the definition risks making

LLDMS a de facto seasonal service during summer and undermining its event-driven design.


       Identifiable extreme weather events are the most suitable trigger for this service given the

nature of the loads it is designed to attract, the advance notice requirements of its design, and the

reliability history that motivated the Legislature to enact PURA § 39.170(b). The Commission

should revise subsection (b)(1) to define "extreme weather condition" as a discrete weather event




                                                  13
 that creates a significant risk for an EEA event or adopt a similarly bounded formulation that

confines the service to its intended statutory purpose.

D.      D.      Large load customers with onsite backup generation should be eligible to
        participate in LLDMS.

        The Commission should expressly permit large load customers with onsite backup

generation to participate in LLDMS. PURA § 37.0561(e) provides that these customers are not

prohibited from providing the service. The rule and ERCOT' s implementing protocols should not

impose eligibility requirements that effectively exclude them in contravention of the statute.

        In the context of eligibility considerations for these loads, the program' s design should

target only those reductions that are incremental to normal operations and demonstrably

attributable to the service' s deployment, rather than reductions that would have occurred anyway.

While these loads are already subj ect to curtailment before firm load shed, in some circumstances

it may make sense to give ERCOT the ability to curtail these loads earlier, or to give ERCOT more

operational control of such loads under a market service. If the objective of PURA § 39.170(b) is

to maximize the incremental megawatts available to ERCOT during an anticipated emergency

condition, then there may be meaningful value in making onsite backup generation capacity

available earlier in the curtailment sequence than it would otherwise be deployed.

        Under existing protocols, this capacity becomes available only after ERCOT deploys all

available market services except frequency-responsive services. Voluntary LLDMS participation

could make some of that demand response available during the critical window between

identifying an anticipated emergency and the onset of firm load shed, giving ERCOT additional

operational flexibility.




                                                 14
        These reliability benefits of earlier access to that capacity justify inclusion of these

customers in the program, subj ect to appropriate safeguards to ensure that compensation is directed

toward resources that provide incremental value.      For example, if a load with onsite backup

generation would have been curtailed at EEA Level 3 under existing protocols, the incremental

value ofLLDMS participation lies in the load's willingness to curtail earlier-potentially hours or

even a day before conditions deteriorate to that level-in response to ERCOT's LLDMS

deployment instruction.

       LLDMS' s interaction with existing curtailment obligations for loads with onsite backup

generation will require careful protocol development.          Through the stakeholder process

contemplated in subsection (i), the Commission should direct ERCOT to establish clear rules

addressing whether and how LLDMS deployment is credited against a load' s existing curtailment

obligation under PURA § 37.0561 and how compensation is calculated when a load curtails earlier

than it otherwise would under existing protocols.


                                     IV.     CONCLUSION

       TIEC appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments on the Proposal for Publication

of new §25.521 and looks forward to continued engagement with Commission Staff and

stakeholders as the LLDMS is finalized. TIEC remains committed to working collaboratively to

ensure the service achieves its statutory obj ectives while protecting consumer interests and

maximizing participation from eligible large loads.

                                    PROJECT NO. 58482

LARGE LOAD DEMAND                             §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
MANAGEMENT SERVICE                            §                OF TEXAS

            TEXAS INDUSTRIAL ENERGY CONSUMERS' COMMENTS
                         EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 •   TIEC appreciates the Commission' s "as-needed" procurement model. LLDMS should be
     a structured, event-driven service that formalizes the voluntary curtailment activities large
     industrial loads have demonstrated during Winter Storms Elliott, Heather, and Fern.

 •   The proposed $5,000/MWh offer cap is too low to attract meaningful participation and
     could undermine LLDMS. The cap should be increased to approximately $20,000/MWh,
     grounded in the system-wide Value of Lost Load.

 •   The $54 million annual budget cap is reasonable as an initial ceiling but should be
     understood as a ceiling, not an expected annual expenditure, with actual spending in most
     years well below the cap and a mechanism for periodic review.

 •   TIEC envisioned that the service would pay for actual deployments , not availability to
     deploy. If the Commission adopts an availability payment, it should be very low (or zero)
     to support a higher deployment payment, with rigorous verification.

 •   ERCOT should use a tiered procurement approach beginning 48-72 hours before an
     anticipated emergency event, and the monthly trigger should be limited to month-ahead
     procurement to prevent ERCOT from procuring LLDMS on a seasonal or annual basis.

 •   The draft rule's definition of "extreme weather condition" is overly broad and should be
     narrowed to a discrete weather event-primarily extreme winter storms. A broad
     definition risks making LLDMS a de facto seasonal service during summer, undermining
     its event-driven design.

 •   Deploying LLDMS for transmission emergencies is not appropriate unless tied to an
     extreme weather event, as PURA § 39.170(b)(1) limits deployment accordingly.

 •   The Commission should avoid over-exclusion that would deter participation: ineligibility
     should apply at the MW level rather than the site level, prior voluntary curtailment should
     not render a load "price-responsive, " and response to 4CP signals should not preclude
     participation because 4CP does not reliably align with emergency conditions.

 •   Large load customers with onsite backup generation should be expressly permitted to
     participate consistent with PURA § 37.0561(e), as there may be meaningful value in
     making that capacity available earlier in the curtailment sequence than existing protocols
     allow.
